summary: Hebrew builds most words from a **root** — usually three consonants that carry a core meaning — poured into a **pattern** of vowels and extra letters that carries the grammar. א־כ־ל means “eat”: אָכַל “he ate”, אוֹכֵל “eats”, לֶאֱכֹל “to eat”, אֹכֶל “food”, מַאֲכָל “a dish”. Verbs come in seven patterns, the **binyanim**; the verbs so far use two. **Paʿal** (also called קַל), the basic one: אָכַל, אָהַב, שָׁתָה, רָצָה, קָנָה — and הָיָה. **Piʿel**: בִּשֵּׁל “to cook” — the middle root letter is doubled (the dot in שּׁ) and the present starts with מְ־: מְבַשֵּׁל. Some root letters are weak: a root ending in ה (שׁ־ת־ה, ר־צ־ה, ק־נ־ה) loses it in many forms (שׁוֹתֶה, שׁוֹתָה, לִשְׁתּוֹת), and the gutturals א, ה, ח, ע take hataf vowels (אוֹהֲבִים, לֶאֱכֹל). Dictionaries list a verb by its past “he” form (אָכַל, בִּשֵּׁל), and many also by the root. Arabic works the same way, often with the same roots: أَكَلَ (ʔakala) “he ate” is א־כ־ל.

blocks.title: Root = meaning, pattern = grammar
blocks.text: Once you know a root, you can guess words you have never seen: from ב־שׁ־ל “cook”, בִּשּׁוּל is “cooking” and בָּשֵׁל “ripe” (cooked by the sun). New verbs are made the same way, by putting a root into a binyan — not with a helper verb: from טֶלֶפוֹן comes the piʿel טִלְפֵּן “he phoned”.

blocks.title: Finding the root
blocks.text: Take away the pattern: the vowel letters ו and י (אוֹכֵל → א־כ־ל), the מְ of the piʿel present (מְבַשֵּׁל → ב־שׁ־ל), the endings -ֶת, -ָה, -ִים, -וֹת and the לְ of the infinitive. What is left — usually three consonants — is the root.

blocks.title: Weak letters hide
blocks.text: A final ה is not written in many forms (שׁוֹתִים, לִשְׁתּוֹת) and a final ה in שׁוֹתֶה / שׁוֹתָה is only the vowel; yet the root is שׁ־ת־ה. Gutturals change the vowels next to them: אוֹהֲבִים, not *אוֹהְבִים.

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Which consonants stay in every form?
Does the present start with מְ־? (piʿel)
Does the root end in ה, or contain א, ה, ח, ע?

askYourself: Which consonants stay in every form? (Ignore ו / י used as vowels, the מְ of the piʿel present, the לְ of the infinitive and the endings.)
Does the present start with מְ־ and is the middle letter doubled? → piʿel; otherwise (like אוֹכֵל) paʿal.
Does the root end in ה? → expect vowel endings: שׁוֹתֶה, שׁוֹתָה, לִשְׁתּוֹת.
Is there a guttural (א, ה, ח, ע)? → expect hataf vowels: אוֹהֲבִים, לֶאֱכֹל.
Looking a verb up? → use its root, or its past “he” form (אָכַל).
steps: Strip the pattern letters and the endings.
Recognise the binyan from the present or the past.

traps: The ו in אוֹכֵל is a vowel letter (o), not part of the root: א־כ־ל.
The מְ of מְבַשֵּׁל belongs to the pattern, not to the root: ב־שׁ־ל.
A binyan is not a tense: paʿal and piʿel each have a past, a present and a future.
Similar letters, different roots: רָצָה “he wanted” (ר־צ־ה) — but הִיא רָצָה “she runs” (ר־ו־ץ).
Not every word has a Semitic root: loans such as סָלָט, קָפֶה, בִּירָה, טֶלֶפוֹן are learned as they are.

quiz.q: Which three letters are the root of אוֹכֶלֶת “(she) eats”?
quiz.why: ו is only the vowel o, and -ֶת is the feminine ending: the root is א־כ־ל, as in אָכַל and אֹכֶל.

quiz.q: Which word shares its root with אָכַל “to eat”?
quiz.why: אֹכֶל has the same three letters א־כ־ל in another pattern; אָהַב is א־ה־ב.
The present starts with מְ־ and the middle root letter is doubled (the dot in שּׁ): piʿel.

quiz.q: Under which form do Hebrew dictionaries list a verb?
quiz.why: The past 3rd person masculine singular is the shortest form with all the root letters — Arabic dictionaries do the same (أَكَلَ).

quiz.q: Why does שׁוֹתָה “(she) drinks” have no -ֶת ending like אוֹכֶלֶת?
options: its root ends in ה, so the feminine ends in -ָה
quiz.answer: its root ends in ה, so the feminine ends in -ָה
quiz.why: Roots ending in ה (שׁ־ת־ה, ר־צ־ה, ק־נ־ה) make the feminine present in -ָה: שׁוֹתָה, רוֹצָה, קוֹנָה.

quiz.q: Which word comes from the root ל־מ־ד “learn”?
quiz.why: תַּלְמִיד “pupil” is תַּ + ל־מ־ד + ־ִי־; מוֹרֶה comes from י־ר־ה, סֵפֶר from ס־פ־ר.

quiz.q: The root ס־פ־ר gives סֵפֶר “book” and also …
quiz.why: סִפּוּר has ס־פ־ר; סֻכָּר and סָלָט are loanwords (from Arabic and from Latin).
Same root, different patterns: ripe fruit is “cooked” by the sun.

quiz.q: Arabic أَكَلَ (ʔakala) “he ate” and Hebrew אָכַל share …
options: a loan from Hebrew into Arabic
quiz.why: Both go back to Proto-Semitic *ʔakal- — roots are shared across the Semitic languages.

seeAlso.note: Arabic is the same system, often with the same roots (أَكَلَ ~ אָכַל); Arabic form II (فَعَّلَ), with a doubled middle letter, matches the Hebrew piʿel (בִּשֵּׁל).
German has no roots and patterns, but its strong verbs change the vowel inside a fixed frame (essen – aß – gegessen) — a small taste of the Semitic idea.
Chinese never changes a word inside: it builds words by joining whole syllables (吃 + 饭 → 吃饭) — the opposite strategy.

notes.text: The same system, often with the same roots: א־כ־ל ~ ء ك ل (أَكَلَ), כ־ת־ב ~ ك ت ب, שׁ־ל־ם ~ س ل م. The binyanim match Arabic verb forms: piʿel ~ form II with a doubled middle letter, hifʿil ~ form IV.
Greek builds words from a stem plus endings and suffixes (γράφω, γράμμα, γραφείο); Hebrew pours three consonants into vowel patterns: א־כ־ל → אָכַל, אוֹכֵל, אֹכֶל.
Russian adds prefixes and suffixes to a stem (писать, писатель, написать); Hebrew keeps the consonants and changes the vowels and pattern letters around them.
Spanish derives with suffixes (cocinar, cocina, cocinero); Hebrew changes the vowel pattern of the root ב־שׁ־ל: בִּשֵּׁל, מְבַשֵּׁל, בִּשּׁוּל.
English sing – sang – song is a small taste of the idea: the consonants stay and the vowels change. In Hebrew this is the main way of making words.
French builds words with suffixes on a stem (cuire, cuisson, cuisine); Hebrew puts a consonant root into patterns.
German singen – sang – gesungen – Gesang changes vowels inside a frame of consonants, as Hebrew does everywhere: אָכַל, אוֹכֵל, אֹכֶל.
Hindi words grow from stems with suffixes; its Arabic loans (किताब) share roots with Hebrew (כ־ת־ב), but Hindi does not change their vowels to make new words.
Persian borrowed many Arabic words together with their patterns (کتاب، کاتب، مکتب), so the root idea is familiar: Hebrew כְּתָב, כּוֹתֵב, מִכְתָּב are built in the same way from כ־ת־ב.
Marathi words grow from stems with suffixes; Hebrew words grow from roots of three consonants placed into vowel patterns.

Turkish keeps the stem and adds suffixes in a row (yaz-, yazar, yazı); Hebrew changes the vowels inside a root and adds letters around it (כ־ת־ב: כָּתַב, כְּתָב, מִכְתָּב). The Arabic loans kitap, katip, mektup come from the same root.
Japanese builds words with suffixes and compounds (食べる, 食べ物); Hebrew changes the vowels around a root: אָכַל “he ate”, אֹכֶל “food”.
Korean adds endings to an unchanging stem (먹다, 먹어요); Hebrew keeps only the consonants fixed: אָכַל, אוֹכֵל, אֹכֶל.
Finnish adds suffixes and changes consonants at the edge of the stem; Hebrew keeps the root consonants and changes the vowels between them.
Hungarian chains suffixes onto a stem; Hebrew changes the vowel pattern around a root.

Swahili keeps the verb root and adds prefixes and suffixes (kupika “to cook”, mpishi “a cook”); Hebrew changes the vowels inside: בִּשֵּׁל, מְבַשֵּׁל, בִּשּׁוּל. The Arabic loan kitabu shares the root כ־ת־ב.
Luganda builds words with class prefixes and verb extensions around a fixed root; Hebrew changes the vowels around three consonants.
Chinese never changes the inside of a word; it joins whole syllables (吃 + 饭 → 吃饭). Hebrew changes the vowels and adds letters around a root: אָכַל, אוֹכֵל, אֹכֶל.
Vietnamese words never change inside; new words are compounds of whole syllables. Hebrew makes new words by changing the vowels around a root.
Inuktitut builds long words by adding suffix after suffix to a stem; Hebrew keeps words short and changes their inside — the vowels around the root consonants.
